promptText: Why is the choice between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read best understood as a decision about which side of the read/write ratio you make expensive, rather than one algorithm simply being faster than the other?
options: Push pays a cost proportional to the author's follower count once, at write time, while pull pays a cost proportional to the reader's followee count on every single read, so the right default depends on which of those two volumes is larger for a given workload
Fan-out-on-write is unconditionally faster in every scenario because it avoids a database query entirely
Fan-out-on-read is unconditionally faster because it never requires a message queue
The choice depends only on which programming language the fan-out worker is written in
explanation: Push moves the distribution cost to write time, proportional to how many followers the author has, while pull defers it to read time, proportional to how many followees the reader has; given that feed reads vastly outnumber writes for most accounts, paying the cost once at write time and reusing the result on every read is cheaper in aggregate, which is why push is the right default for the common case rather than an absolute winner.

promptText: Why does a per-user feed use a Redis sorted set keyed by timestamp rather than a plain list or a row-per-entry relational table?
options: A sorted set keeps entries ordered automatically on every insert, so fetching the most recent N post IDs is a direct range read (ZREVRANGE) instead of a sort-then-limit step repeated on every request
A sorted set is the only Redis structure that supports time-to-live expiration on individual members
A relational table cannot store an integer post ID, so a key-value structure is mandatory
A plain list would require the feed cache to be replicated across every region, while a sorted set would not
explanation: A sorted set maintains order by score as a property of the data structure itself, so the newest posts are always retrievable with a cheap range operation; a plain list would require the application to maintain ordering manually, and a relational row-per-entry table would force a sort-and-limit query on every single read, which is exactly the repeated cost precomputing the feed is meant to avoid.

promptText: Why does the feed cache store only post IDs rather than the full serialized post content?
options: It keeps fan-out writes small and cheap regardless of post size, and it lets a post be edited, moderated, or deleted by updating one authoritative row instead of every feed cache that already copied its content
Redis sorted sets are physically incapable of storing values larger than an 8-byte integer
Storing full content would make the feed impossible to paginate with a cursor
Post IDs are required so that the ranking model can compute engagement scores
explanation: Fanning out a post to a million feeds means inserting a million small (ID, score) pairs rather than copying the full post body a million times, which keeps write cost and storage bounded; it also means an edit or moderation action only has to touch the single authoritative post store, since every feed cache resolves the current content at read time via hydration.

promptText: Why does an infinite-scroll feed need cursor-based pagination instead of classic LIMIT/OFFSET paging?
options: A feed keeps receiving new items ahead of the reader's current position, so an offset that pointed at the right rows on page one points at a shifted set of rows by the time page two is requested, silently skipping or duplicating items
Offset-based pagination cannot be implemented against a Redis sorted set under any circumstances
Cursor-based pagination removes the need for the feed cache to be sharded across nodes
LIMIT/OFFSET queries are rejected by the post store once a table exceeds a few million rows
explanation: Offset paging assumes the ordering stays stable between requests, but a feed is a moving target that keeps inserting new items ahead of the reader's position, so the same offset resolves to different rows on the next page; a cursor anchored to a specific point in the ordering (a timestamp or score the client already saw) stays correct no matter what gets inserted ahead of it.

promptText: Why must post creation return to the client before fan-out to followers has actually happened, rather than blocking until fan-out completes?
options: Fan-out cost is proportional to the author's follower count, so blocking on it would make a normal post's latency fine but a high-follower account's post latency scale with millions of writes, sometimes minutes
Blocking on fan-out would violate the database's unique constraint on post IDs
The post store cannot accept a write unless the message queue is reachable first
Returning immediately is only necessary because Redis does not support transactions
explanation: If the post-creation request waited for fan-out to finish, its latency would directly depend on the author's follower count, which is fine for a few hundred followers but means a high-follower account's post could take minutes to acknowledge; decoupling fan-out onto an asynchronous queue keeps post-creation latency independent of follower count entirely.

promptText: A single post goes viral and ends up referenced by millions of feed caches. What specifically keeps the authoritative post-content store from being overwhelmed as those feeds hydrate it?
options: A hot-content cache sits in front of the post store, so once the viral post is cached, millions of hydration requests are served from that fast cache layer instead of hitting the backing store individually
The post store automatically replicates a post to every shard the instant it is created
The feed cache stores the full post content for viral posts specifically, bypassing hydration entirely
Consistent hashing on the post ID guarantees the post can never become a hot key
explanation: This is the same hot-key caching pattern applied to post content: placing a cache in front of the authoritative store means a popular post is served from cache on nearly every hydration rather than hitting the backing store each time, converting what would otherwise be a database bottleneck into a cache-hit-dominated workload.

promptText: A fan-out worker fleet sustains roughly 200,000 feed-cache writes per second. Why does a single post from a 50-million-follower account amount to more than just extra latency for that account's own followers?
options: Propagating that one post consumes the fleet's entire sustained write capacity for about 250 seconds, so every other normal-account post queued behind it during that window is delayed too, degrading fan-out platform-wide, not only for that account's followers
It only affects the celebrity's own followers, since fan-out workers process each account's followers on an isolated queue partition
The delay is purely cosmetic because the post is already visible in the author's own post history
It is resolved automatically by the social graph being sharded by user_id
explanation: 50 million writes at 200,000 writes/second take about 250 seconds, during which that one post is consuming the fan-out fleet's entire throughput; any normal post queued behind it in that same window gets delayed as a side effect, so the blast radius extends to unrelated users' posts, not just to the celebrity's own follower base.

promptText: In the hybrid model, why does a celebrity's post skip write-time fan-out entirely instead of simply spreading the same fan-out writes out over a longer time window?
options: Spreading writes out reduces the instantaneous spike but still performs the same total number of writes and leaves followers in inconsistent states mid-rollout, whereas skipping fan-out and merging at read time replaces that total write cost with a handful of cheap lookups paid only by readers who actually check their feed
Spreading fan-out writes over time is what the hybrid model actually does for celebrity accounts, in place of a read-time overlay
Celebrity posts are simply dropped and never shown to any follower under the hybrid model
Rate-limiting the celebrity's posting frequency eliminates the need for any fan-out decision at all
explanation: A spread-out fan-out still eventually performs all 50 million writes and creates a window where some followers have the post and others don't with no clean cutoff; pulling the post in at read time instead means the total work done shrinks to a small number of lookups, incurred only by the subset of followers who actually open their feed, which is strictly less total work, not just the same work smoothed out.

promptText: How does consistent hashing specifically protect the feed-cache cluster as the system scales out?
options: Each user's feed cache entry is placed on the ring by hashing user_id, so adding or removing cache nodes only reshuffles the small fraction of users whose keys land near the new node's ring position, instead of remapping nearly every user at once
It guarantees that no feed cache entry is ever evicted regardless of memory pressure
It is the mechanism used to decide whether an account has crossed the celebrity threshold
It replaces the need to shard the social graph store by user_id
explanation: Consistent hashing on user_id bounds how much data moves when the cache cluster is resized: only keys near the new node's position on the ring are reassigned, whereas naive modulo hashing would change nearly every key's owning node and trigger a rehashing storm across the fan-out pipeline exactly when capacity is being added to relieve load.

promptText: A user follows a new account. Why doesn't that account's older posts automatically appear in the new follower's feed cache?
options: Fan-out only inserts a post into a follower's feed cache at the moment that post is created, so a follow relationship created afterward never triggers fan-out for posts that already happened, unless the system explicitly backfills or treats the followee as a celebrity temporarily
The feed cache automatically performs a full historical fan-out the instant a new follow relationship is recorded
Older posts are excluded because the post store deletes content older than the feed cache's bounded length
This only happens if the followee is a celebrity account; normal accounts backfill instantly by default
explanation: Fan-out-on-write is triggered by post creation events, not by follow events, so a brand-new follow relationship has no past PostCreated events to react to; a correct design either backfills a bounded number of the followee's recent posts at follow time or treats the followee like a celebrity for a short grace period, otherwise the new follower sees nothing until the next post.

promptText: A post is deleted after it has already been fanned out into millions of feed caches. What is the standard way to handle the now-stale post ID references?
options: Let the hydration step silently drop any post ID that no longer resolves to live content when assembling a page, rather than synchronously scrubbing every feed cache that ever referenced it
Synchronously scan and remove the post ID from every feed cache it was fanned out to before returning success for the deletion
Reject the deletion request until all feed caches referencing the post have expired naturally
Trigger a full resharding of the feed-cache cluster so the deleted post's shard is rebuilt
explanation: Synchronously scrubbing millions of feed caches the instant a post is deleted would be expensive and doesn't scale with fan-out volume, so the standard approach lets the hydration step detect that an ID no longer resolves to live content and drop it from the returned page, which handles deletion correctly without touching the feed caches themselves at all.

promptText: Why is the social graph store sharded by user_id rather than by some other key, and why does that choice matter for both the fan-out and the read path?
options: Sharding by user_id lets "who do I follow" and "who follows me" resolve on a single shard, which both the fan-out worker (follower lookup) and the feed read path (celebrity-follow overlay) depend on being fast and avoiding a cross-shard scatter-gather
Sharding by user_id is required because Redis sorted sets cannot be queried across shard boundaries
Sharding by user_id eliminates the celebrity problem by distributing a celebrity's followers evenly across shards
Sharding by user_id is only relevant to the post store, not to the social graph
explanation: Both fan-out (which needs an author's full follower list) and feed reads (which need a reader's followee list and celebrity-follow subset) hinge on graph lookups that are cheap only if they resolve on one shard; sharding by user_id gives both paths that single-shard property, whereas a key that didn't align with these access patterns would force an expensive scatter-gather across shards on every fan-out and every read.

promptText: Why must the fan-out worker check an author's follower count against the celebrity threshold fresh on every post, instead of relying on a value cached at account-creation time?
options: Follower counts can grow rapidly, so a stale cached count could leave a now-huge account routed through write-time fan-out, triggering exactly the write-amplification spike the threshold exists to prevent, at the moment the account's post reaches the most readers
Caching the follower count at account creation is actually the recommended approach, since follower counts rarely change meaningfully after an account is created
The celebrity threshold check only needs to run once per day via a scheduled batch job, independent of individual posts
Follower count is irrelevant to the fan-out decision; only the post's content length determines whether fan-out proceeds
explanation: An account can go viral and cross the celebrity threshold within hours, so a decision based on a stale, account-creation-time follower count would still push-fan-out a post from an account that has since become huge, producing the exact write-amplification spike the hybrid model exists to avoid; evaluating current follower count per post closes that gap.

promptText: The product now requires that a user always sees their own newly created post at the top of their own feed immediately, even though normal fan-out is asynchronous and eventually consistent. How should the design accommodate this without abandoning the asynchronous architecture for everyone else?
options: Special-case the author's own view of their own feed to read directly from the durable post store (or a cache populated synchronously at write time), since the eventual-consistency guarantee only needs to hold for other users' feeds, not the author's immediate view of their own post
Make the entire post-creation path synchronous so that fan-out to every follower completes before the request returns
Add a global lock around the fan-out pipeline so no other post can be processed until the author's own feed read confirms the new post
Nothing needs to change, because the asynchronous fan-out pipeline already guarantees the author sees their own post instantly by design
explanation: The eventual-consistency trade-off (Section 3.2) was adopted for propagation to other users' feeds, not for the author's own view of their own content, so the narrow fix is to special-case the author's own feed/profile read to bypass the async fan-out pipeline entirely; making the whole system synchronous would reintroduce the exact write-latency-proportional-to-followers problem the queue exists to remove.

promptText: An account sits right at the celebrity threshold and repeatedly gains and loses followers around that exact number across consecutive posts. What is the correct way to prevent this from destabilizing the fan-out pipeline?
options: Add hysteresis: only switch the account to celebrity (pull) mode once it exceeds the threshold by a margin, and only switch it back to normal (push) mode once it drops meaningfully below that margin, backfilling the feed cache when it moves back to push mode
Apply the exact same single threshold value in both directions with no margin, since simplicity matters more than avoiding occasional mode switches
Permanently classify the account as a celebrity the first time it ever crosses the threshold, even if its follower count later drops well below it
Disable fan-out entirely for any account within a fixed range of the threshold until its follower count stabilizes for a full quarter
explanation: Without hysteresis, an account oscillating right at the boundary could flip between push and pull fan-out strategies on every post, which is wasted engineering and operational complexity for no real benefit; adding a margin on each side of the threshold, plus a backfill step when moving back to push mode, keeps the fan-out decision stable without needing a permanent, irreversible classification.
